p: Bərhanat means lights. Older English says luminaries. The word comes from Genesis 1.
b: The Ge'ez bərhanat means simply "lights." Older English translations say "luminaries." The word points back to Genesis 1:14–16, where God makes "lights" to mark "the appointed times, the days and the years" (Genesis 1:14). The opening words give this work its old names: the Book of the Luminaries, or the Astronomical Book. It treats the sun, moon and stars as made things that keep God's law, not as gods.
orig: መጽሐፈ ሚጠተ ብርሃናተ ሰማይ (mäṣḥäfä miṭätä bərhanatä sämay), "book of the turnings of the lights of heaven"

p: The angel whose name means "God is my light" is the guide of the lights.
b: Ge'ez ʾUrʾel is the Hebrew name Uriel, "God is my light" or "my light is God." The name fits his job: he is in charge of the lights (75:3; 82:7). He is one of the holy angels listed in 20:2, and he guides Enoch on earlier tours too (see 21:5; 33:3–4). In 4 Ezra he is the angel who answers Ezra's questions (4 Ezra 4:1). The 66 books name only two angels, Michael and Gabriel (Daniel 8:16; Daniel 10:13; Luke 1:19); Raphael appears in Tobit (Tobit 3:17).

a: until the new creation is made that will last forever
t: The order lasts until the new creation
p: The sky's laws last only until God makes all things new: a hope the prophets and the New Testament share.
b: The book's very first sentence sets a limit on the order it describes: it runs "until the new creation is made." Isaiah promises "new heavens and a new earth" (Isaiah 65:17; Isaiah 66:22), and the New Testament takes up the hope (2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1; compare 2 Corinthians 5:17). Later parts of 1 Enoch use the same picture (see 91:16). The astronomy is not an end in itself: it describes the world God will one day renew.

t: Shamash and the gates of heaven
p: In Babylon the sun god stepped through doors in the eastern mountain. Enoch keeps the gates and drops the god.
b: Babylonian seals show the sun god Shamash stepping through the doors of the eastern mountain at dawn. Babylonian astronomy (the MUL.APIN compendium, compiled before about 700 BC) tracked where the sun and moon rose along the horizon over the year. Most scholars think Enoch's scheme of gates comes from this learned Babylonian tradition, passed on to Jewish scribes in the Persian or early Greek period. Verdict: a real link through astronomy, not borrowed worship. In Enoch the gates are only openings; the sun is a made thing driven by wind and guided by an angel.

a: six gates where the sun comes out
p: The six gates divide the stretch of horizon where the sun rises over a year.
b: Watch the sunrise for a year and you see it move along the eastern horizon: far to the southeast in midwinter, far to the northeast in midsummer. Enoch splits that stretch into six "gates." Gate 1 is the southern end (midwinter), gate 6 the northern end (midsummer). The sun spends a month in each gate going north and a month coming back south. Six gates in the west match them. Marking the sunrise against the horizon is one of the oldest ways of keeping a calendar.

p: The stars move like an army with officers, a picture the Bible also uses.
b: The Ge'ez märaḥyan (Dillmann has the singular form märaḥi) means "leaders, guides." The stars march like troops behind their officers. Isaiah says God "brings out their army by number" and calls each by name (Isaiah 40:26), and Job speaks of leading out the constellations (Job 38:31–33). 1 Enoch names these leaders in 82:9–20.

a: Its circle is like the circle of the sky
p: The phrase is puzzling: it may mean the sun's disk, or the path it travels.
b: Kəbäb means a circle or its rim. Read flatly, the sun is as wide as the sky, which cannot be meant, since 72:37 and 78:3 make the sun and moon the same size. Scholars suggest the phrase describes the sun's round disk, or the circle of its yearly path around the sky. The same words come again for the moon (73:2) and for both lights (78:3).
orig: ክበቡ ከመ ክበበ ሰማይ (kəbäbu kämä kəbäbä sämay)

a: The wind drives the chariot it rides up in
p: Greeks pictured Helios driving horses across the sky. Here wind pushes and an angel guides.
b: Greek poets pictured the god Helios driving a chariot with fiery horses across the sky. Judah's kings once kept "chariots of the sun" at the temple, and Josiah burned them (2 Kings 23:11). Enoch keeps the chariot but takes away the god: wind drives it, and it is "guided" by God's appointed order. Verdict: a shared ancient picture, used so that no one would worship the sun (compare 80:7).

a: goes back around through the north
t: Compared with the Bible: how the sky works
p: The Bible uses the same everyday picture but never explains the machinery. Enoch claims to.
b: Enoch pictures a flat earth: the sun sets in the west and travels back behind the north to rise again in the east (compare 78:5). The Bible speaks the same everyday way ("The sun rises and the sun goes down, and hurries back to its place," Ecclesiastes 1:5; compare Psalm 19:6), but it never teaches how the sky works. Enoch goes beyond the Bible by presenting the mechanism as an angel's revelation. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers say the book describes the sky as people see it, as the Bible itself does. Most other churches see the outdated astronomy as one reason not to read the book as Scripture.

p: The first month starts at the spring equinox, as in the Torah's calendar.
b: The year opens with the sun in gate 4, just after the spring equinox, when day and night are equal. That matches the Torah, where the year's first month is the spring month of Passover (Exodus 12:2; Leviticus 23:5). Why gate 4 is "great" is not said; perhaps because the year starts there. Like the Torah's priestly texts, Enoch numbers the months instead of naming them.

p: Each gate has windows, and flame comes out of them in season: that is how Enoch explains summer heat.
b: The windows explain why the days get hotter: in their season they open and let out flame. 75:4–7 returns to these windows. The Bible speaks of "the windows of the heavens" for rain (Genesis 7:11; Malachi 3:10); Enoch adds windows for heat, so that every kind of weather has its proper opening.

p: Enoch counts days as "mornings." Some think this tradition began the day at dawn.
b: The Ge'ez counts ṣəbaḥ, "mornings," not days. The sun is the timekeeper, so each new appearance of the sun is one unit. Some scholars, such as Talmon, argued that the groups who used this calendar began the day at sunrise, unlike the later Jewish practice of starting at sunset (based on "evening and morning," Genesis 1:5). Others think the evidence is too thin to tell.

p: Day and night together are 18 parts. Each part is 80 minutes.
b: Enoch splits a full day and night into 18 parts, so each part is 80 of our minutes. Here the day has 10 parts and the night 8, so the day is longer by two parts. The Ge'ez kaʿbätä means "double" or "twofold": "longer by a double measure," which matches the two-part gap. Charles wrote "by a ninth part," since 2 of 18 parts is one ninth of the whole. 72:18 counts the change the same way (10 against 8).

p: The day grows from 10 parts to 11, yet the Ge'ez says "two parts."
b: The Ge'ez says the day grows "two parts" (EOTC kəlʾetä ʾədä; Dillmann's digitized numeral is evidently ፪, "two"). Yet the day was 10 parts at the end of the first month (72:10) and is now 11, a gain of one. The "two" may be counted from the equinox (9 to 11), as 72:18 counts from midsummer (12 to 10), or it may be a slip. The matching verse on the way back, 72:16, says "shorter by exactly one part." The Plain keeps the Ge'ez.

p: Every third month has a 31st day, its "sign." These are the four added days of the year.
b: In months 3, 6, 9 and 12 the sun stays 31 mornings in its gate, "because of its sign" (72:13, 19, 25, 31). Twelve months of 30 days make 360; these four extra days bring the year to 364 (72:32). They fall at the turning points of the year: midsummer, the autumn equinox, midwinter and the spring equinox. 75:1–2 and 82:4–6 explain that people go wrong by leaving them out.
orig: በእንተ ትእምርተ ዚአሃ (bäʾənətä təʾmərtä ziʾäha), "because of its sign"

a: twice as long as the night
p: Twelve parts of eighteen is 16 hours: too long for Jerusalem. The ratio comes from Babylon.
b: Twelve parts out of eighteen is two thirds of 24 hours: a longest day of 16 hours and a shortest night of 8. In Jerusalem the longest day is only about 14 hours. A 16-hour day is true only far to the north, around 49° latitude (Neugebauer). The 2 to 1 ratio is the scheme of Babylonian astronomy, found in MUL.APIN, but it does not fit Babylon either: at Babylon (about 32½°) the longest day is about 14½ hours. So the numbers are a learned scheme, inherited and kept, not measurements taken anywhere in the Near East.

p: The Ge'ez says the sun's "heads," probably the points where its path turns.
b: ʾArʾəst is the plural of "head." Here it seems to mean the stations or turning points of the sun's path: the places where it starts a new month. Charles wrote "the divisions of his orbit." The same word stands in 72:29.

a: The year comes to exactly 364 days.
p: 364 days is exactly 52 weeks, so every date falls on the same weekday every year.
b: Add up the chapter: twelve months of 30 days, plus four 31st days, makes 364. That is exactly 52 weeks. So in this calendar every date falls on the same day of the week every year, and no feast ever falls on a Sabbath unless the calendar puts it there on purpose. Jubilees makes the same year a command (Jubilees 6:32), and many Dead Sea Scrolls use it. The real solar year is about 365¼ days, so a 364-day calendar slips about a day and a quarter each year. How its users dealt with that, if they did, is unknown.

t: Compared with the Bible: the length of the year
p: The Bible never states how long the year is. Enoch says an angel revealed it: 364 days.
b: The Bible says God made the lights to "mark the appointed times, the days and the years" (Genesis 1:14), but it never gives the year's length. Its months follow the moon: the word for month, chodesh, means "new moon," and new moons had their own offerings (Numbers 28:11). Its feasts are tied to harvests (Exodus 23:16), which a 364-day year would drift away from within a few decades. So Enoch goes beyond the Bible here, and many readers think it conflicts with the Bible's moon-based months. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church, which counts the book as Scripture, has never used this year: its own calendar has 365 days (366 in leap years): twelve months of 30 days and a short thirteenth month of 5 or 6 days.

p: Genesis has the lights "keep the day apart from the night"; Enoch shows how.
b: In Genesis the lights are made "to keep the day apart from the night" (Genesis 1:14), and after the flood God promises that "day and night" will not stop (Genesis 8:22). Psalm 104 says the moon marks the seasons and the sun knows when to set (Psalm 104:19). Enoch spells out what those verses only state: the sun's course makes days and nights longer and shorter.

p: The number is a puzzle. One possible sense: sixty days a year in each middle gate.
b: The EOTC print spells out "sixty" (səsa), and Dillmann's digitized text has the numeral ፷ (60). The sense is unclear; Charles kept it as "sixty times." The numerals ፮ (6) and ፷ (60) are easily confused: in 72:6 and 72:14 the digitized Dillmann text has ፷ where the EOTC spells out "six." So a reading "six," for the six gates, cannot be ruled out, though no manuscript is reported with it. Another possible sense is given in the next note.

p: Claude's suggestion: "sixty" may count the days the sun spends in each gate in a year.
b: My suggestion, not one I have found in print: "sixty" may count days, not returns. The sun spends two months in each gate every year, once going north and once coming back (72:8–31): 60 days in gates 2 and 5, and 61 in gates 1, 3, 4 and 6, which each hold one of the 31-day months. A round "sixty" for "two months in each gate" would fit the chapter's way of counting. This is a guess, offered beside the possibility of "six" in the previous note.

p: Ge'ez ʾƎgziʾ is "the Lord." The lights are named and placed by God's command.
b: ʾƎgziʾ means "lord" and is the usual Ge'ez word for God as Lord; the Plain writes "the Lord." ("The LORD" in capitals is kept for the Hebrew name YHWH, which Ge'ez does not use.) The lights get their names by God's command, as in Psalm 148, where sun, moon and stars praise him "for he gave the order, and they were created" (Psalm 148:3–5), and in Isaiah 40:26, where he calls the stars by name.

a: seven times brighter than the moon's
p: Enoch makes the sun seven times brighter than the moon. Isaiah used the same number for the future.
b: The moon's full light is one seventh of the sun's (73:3; compare 78:4). Isaiah uses the number seven for the day God heals his people: "the light of the sun will be sevenfold" (Isaiah 30:26). Enoch's seven is not a promise but a fixed rule of the sky.

a: in size the two are equal
p: Seen from earth, sun and moon do look the same size, as eclipses show.
b: To the eye the sun and moon are almost exactly the same size; that is why the moon can cover the sun in a total eclipse. Genesis calls them "the two big lights" but makes one "the bigger light" and the other "the smaller light" (Genesis 1:16), and 73:1 uses the same contrast. Enoch's point is that they differ in brightness, not in size (78:3).

a: another law, for the smaller light
t: The Aramaic is much longer here
p: Behind chapters 73–74 stands a long Aramaic table of the moon, day by day. The Ge'ez keeps only a summary.
b: The oldest copies of this book, the Aramaic scrolls 4Q208 and 4Q209 from Qumran Cave 4, contain a long "synchronistic calendar": a day-by-day table of how much of the moon is lit and where it rises and sets, month after month, beside the sun. 4Q208 is copied in a hand dated to about 200 BC, and it seems to have held only this table. The Ethiopic chapters 73–74 read like a short summary of it. So the Ge'ez reader sees only a sketch of what the first readers studied in full.

p: Genesis names it the same way: "the smaller light to govern the night."
b: Ge'ez nəʾus means "small." Genesis 1:16 calls the moon "the smaller light to govern the night," and this chapter follows that wording, as the Plain here does too.

a: light is given to it by measure
t: Where the moon's light comes from
p: Enoch knows the moon's light comes from the sun, given out bit by bit.
b: The moon does not make its own light: it is "given" by measure, and 78:10–11 adds that the sun passes it over. Greek thinkers such as Anaxagoras (400s BC) also taught that the moon shines by the sun's light. Enoch describes it as light being "transferred" day by day, a way of counting the phases rather than a theory of reflection.

a: Its first appearance in the east comes on the thirtieth morning
p: Does the month start at the dark new moon or at the full moon? Scholars still argue.
b: A month can be started at the moment the moon is dark, at the first thin crescent seen after sunset, or (in some schemes) at the full moon. Enoch's description is hard to fit to any of these, since a new crescent appears in the west in the evening, not "in the east." Scholars debate whether this book, and the Qumran calendar texts that build on it, began the month with the dark moon or with the full moon. The rabbis later fixed the month by witnesses who saw the first crescent (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 2:5–8).

a: the fourteenth part of its light
p: Enoch splits the moon into 14 parts (halves of sevenths) and adds one part a day.
b: The moon's light is counted in sevenths and their halves, that is, in fourteenths: Ge'ez "seven and seven parts" (73:6; 73:8; 74:3). Each day the lit part grows by one fourteenth until the moon is full, then shrinks the same way (73:5–8; 74:3; 78:6–8). The Ge'ez fractions in 73:5–8 are tangled, and Dillmann's text and the EOTC print differ in some numbers (see 73:7). Neugebauer showed that the scheme works if one reads every step as one fourteenth of the moon.
orig: ዐሠርቱ ወአርባዕቱ እድ (EOTC, ʿäśärtu wäʾärbaʿtu ʾəd), "fourteen parts"

a: one part of fourteen, and a half
p: Ge'ez "one of seven-and-seven parts, and its half." Charles: "one-seventh part and the half thereof."
b: Dillmann has ፯ወ፯እደ አሐቲ ወመንፈቃ and the EOTC säbʿätu säbʿätä ʾəd ʾäḥäti wämänfäqa: "one of seven-and-seven parts, and its half." The Plain reads "seven and seven" as fourteen, as in 73:8 and 74:3, following Neugebauer's scheme of daily steps of one fourteenth. Charles rendered "one-seventh part and the half thereof."

p: Jewish tradition made Enoch the first to write down the signs of the sky.
b: Genesis says only that Enoch lived 365 years, the number of days in a solar year, and that he "walked with God" (Genesis 5:23–24). Jubilees says he was the first person to learn writing and to write down "the signs of heaven" so that people would know the seasons (Jubilees 4:17–18). A Jewish writer quoted by Eusebius (Pseudo-Eupolemus) says Enoch discovered astronomy and learned it from angels. This chapter is the source of that picture.

p: Both Ge'ez texts say "seven-seven parts." The Plain takes it as fourteenths; Charles as single sevenths.
b: Dillmann reads በ፩ ፯፯እድ ... ወበበ ፯፯እድ and the EOTC bäʾäḥädu säbʿätä säbʿätä ʾədä ... wäbäbä säbʿätu säbʿätu ʾəd: "by one, seven-seven parts ... and by seven-seven parts." The two texts agree. Charles took the doubled number as "in single seventh parts"; the Plain takes "seven and seven" as fourteen, so that the moon fills by fourteenths, following Neugebauer and matching 73:5–8 and the fourteen days of 78:6.
orig: በ፩ ፯፯እድ (Dillmann); በአሐዱ ሰብዐተ ሰብዐተ እደ (EOTC)

a: In some months it changes where it sets
p: The moon sweeps through the gates in a month, as the sun does in a year.
b: The sun takes a year to move from gate 1 to gate 6 and back. The moon makes the same swing in about a month, so in a single month it can rise in the sun's gate, move to the far end and come back (74:5–8). That is true to the sky: the moon's rising point swings north and south much faster than the sun's.

a: run ahead by six days a year
p: A moon year of 354 days is ten days short of 364, but this verse says six.
b: Twelve moon months make about 354 days, ten fewer than 364; 74:14–16 count it that way (50 days in 5 years, 80 in 8). The "six days" here make sense only against a round 360-day year (360 − 354 = 6). Either the verse measures from 360, or two counts have been mixed in the long copying of the text. Neugebauer thought verses 10–11 confused.

a: The moon brings in the years for them exactly
p: The Ge'ez says "the moon," but the verse describes the sun and stars. Charles wrote "the sun and the stars."
b: Both Dillmann's text and the EOTC print begin with "the moon" (wärḫ). Yet the rest of the verse describes lights that never fall behind by a day and finish the year in 364 days: that is the sun and the stars, as 74:11 just said. Charles rendered "the sun and the stars." The Plain keeps the Ge'ez; it may mean that the moon's months are counted out against the sun's years, or it may be an early slip.
orig: ወወርኅ ያመጽኦሙ (wäwärḫ yamäṣʾomu), "and the moon brings them"

a: In three years their days are 1,092
p: After three years the moon is 30 days behind: add a month, and sun and moon line up again.
b: Three years of 364 days are 1,092 days; three moon years of 354 are 1,062 (74:14). The gap is 30 days, exactly one month. So adding one month every three years keeps the moon in step with the 364-day year. The Qumran calendar scrolls (4Q319–4Q321) work this out in six-year cycles and fit the twenty-four priestly divisions into them: 6 × 52 weeks = 312 weeks = 13 turns of the 24 divisions.

a: in eight years there are 2,912 days
p: Greek astronomers also used an eight-year cycle to line up sun and moon.
b: Eight years of 364 days are 2,912 days; eight moon years are 2,832 (74:15), 80 days less (74:16). An eight-year cycle, the octaeteris, was the standard way Greek cities lined up their moon months with the solar year. Its appearance here may show contact with Greek reckoning, though the numbers themselves are simple multiplication of Enoch's own years.

a: it is added to the 62 days
p: The last clause is obscure. It may restate 1,062, or point ahead to the eight-year total.
b: The Ge'ez ends "for by its going out it is added upon 62 days" (Dillmann ፰ወ፪ is evidently ፷ወ፪, 62; the EOTC spells out sixty-two). Charles filled out the sense with words in brackets: to the five-year sum of 1,770 one adds 1,000 and 62, that is 1,062, to reach the eight-year total of 2,832 (74:15). Another possible reading takes the clause as a scribe's note spelling out 1,062 itself. The Plain keeps the Ge'ez wording; the verse's numbers do not depend on it.
orig: ይትዌሰክ ዲበ ስሳ ወክልኤቱ መዋዕል (yətwesäk dibä səsa wäkləʾetu mäwaʿl)

a: the four days that are added
p: Four days stand outside the twelve 30-day months. Enoch insists they belong in the year.
b: Many ancient calendars used an ideal year of 360 days: twelve months of 30. Babylonian astronomy worked with it, and Egypt added five extra days to reach 365. Enoch's four extra days come one at the end of each quarter (72:13). They are "not counted" in the reckoning of the months, yet the angels serve on them, and Enoch says leaving them out is a mistake (75:2; 82:5). The polemic seems aimed at people who counted only 360 days, or who followed the moon.

p: A military title: the stars are an army with officers over units of a thousand.
b: ʾArʾəstä ʾäʾlaf, "heads of thousands," is an army rank. Moses appoints "officers over thousands" in Israel (Exodus 18:21), and Numbers speaks of commanders of thousands (Numbers 31:14). The "army of the sky" (Deuteronomy 4:19) is organized like Israel's camp. 82:11–20 names some of these officers.

a: people make mistakes about these days
p: For the Enoch circle, getting the calendar wrong was not a small error. It was a sin.
b: Enoch says people "go wrong" (the Ge'ez verb gegäyä, here yəgegyu, also means "to sin") about these days. Jubilees warns that Israel will forget the true year and keep the feasts on the wrong days (Jubilees 6:34–38). The Damascus Document from Qumran speaks of "the hidden things in which all Israel went astray: his holy Sabbaths and his glorious feasts" (Damascus Document 3:13–15). A pesher on Habakkuk says the "Wicked Priest" attacked the Teacher of Righteousness on the Teacher's Day of Atonement (1QpHab 11:4–8), which only makes sense if the two kept different calendars.

p: The Ge'ez says "world" (ʿaläm) where the sense needs "year."
b: Three times in this verse ("the stations of the world," "the exactness of the world," "the stations of the world") and again in 82:5 the Ge'ez has ʿaläm, "world, age," where the sense seems to be "year." Why is not known. One possible explanation, a guess: the Hebrew and Aramaic word ʿolam means both "world" and "long age," and a translator could have slid from "age" to "period" or "year." The Plain keeps "world" in the first phrase and writes "year" where only that makes sense.
orig: ምንባረ ዓለም (mənbarä ʿaläm), "stations of the world"

a: the signs, the seasons, the years and the days
p: The list comes from Genesis 1:14. Paul uses a similar list in Galatians 4:10.
b: God made the lights to be "signs" and to "mark the appointed times, the days and the years" (Genesis 1:14), and Enoch repeats the list. Paul warns the Galatians that they "observe days and months and seasons and years" (Galatians 4:10). Scholars debate whether Paul has Jewish calendars like Enoch's in mind or the pagan calendar the Galatians came from; either way, Enoch shows how much weight some Jews put on keeping the right days.

p: A title used in 1 Enoch and once by Paul.
b: Ge'ez ʾƎgziʾa səbḥat. Psalm 24 calls God "the King of glory" (Psalm 24:7–10), as Enoch does in 81:3. Paul calls Jesus "the Lord of glory" (1 Corinthians 2:8), and James uses a similar phrase (James 2:1).

a: has set forever over all the lights of the sky
t: Compared with the Bible: an angel over the stars
p: The Bible links angels and stars, but never names an angel in charge of them. Enoch does.
b: The Bible calls the stars "the whole army of the sky" (Deuteronomy 4:19), has them sing at creation (Job 38:7), and pictures angels over parts of nature: "the angel of the waters" (Revelation 16:5), an angel "who has authority over the fire" (Revelation 14:18). So Enoch agrees with the Bible that God governs the sky through servants, and goes beyond it in naming Uriel as their chief. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church honors Uriel (Urael) as an archangel with his own feast days. The Catholic Church discourages giving angels names other than Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, which come from Scripture (Directory on Popular Piety and the Liturgy, 2001, §217); most Protestants accept only Michael and Gabriel.

p: The Ge'ez calls the sun's rays its "feet."
b: The word is ʾəgäriha, "its feet": the rays are pictured as legs or feet reaching down from the sun to the earth. Egyptian art of the 1300s BC shows the sun disk with rays ending in hands. The Plain gives the plain sense, "rays."
orig: እገሪሃ ለጸሐይ (ʾəgäriha läṣäḥäy), "the feet of the sun"

p: The stars near the pole circle all night and never go down: Enoch sees them riding in chariots.
b: Some stars near the north pole of the sky never set; they wheel around the pole all night. The brightest group, the Big Dipper, was called "the Wagon" by Babylonians and Greeks, which may explain Enoch's "chariots" and the one "greater than all the others" (75:9; compare "the great chariot" in 80:5). Job names the Bear among the constellations God leads (Job 9:9; Job 38:32).

a: twelve gates open for all the winds
p: Enoch names twelve winds, three for each direction, as some Greek writers did.
b: The Bible speaks of "the four winds" (Daniel 7:2; Zechariah 6:5). Enoch splits each of the four into three, making twelve, and says what each brings. Greek writers also counted a dozen winds (Aristotle, Meteorology 2.6). Parts of chapters 76–77 survive in Aramaic in the Qumran scrolls 4Q209 and 4Q210, so this section was part of the book from early on (Milik; Drawnel). By their reports the Aramaic of 76–79 is often fuller than the Ge'ez and sometimes worded differently. This edition records only the 77:1 difference, from Milik's report, because the editions could not be checked here.

a: three on the right of the sky and three on the left
t: Right is south, left is north
p: Facing the sunrise, your right hand points south and your left points north.
b: Hebrew, Aramaic and Ge'ez orient by facing east, toward the sunrise. So "the front" is east, "the right" (yämän; Hebrew yamin, teman) is south, and "the left" is north. Psalm 89:12 pairs "north and south" with the Hebrew words for these sides. 76:3 says "on the left, toward the south," which does not fit this rule; the Ge'ez there may be confused.
orig: የማነ ሰማይ (yämanä sämay), "the right of the sky"

p: Revelation's angels hold back four winds that would harm land and sea.
b: Eight of Enoch's twelve winds bring harm. In Revelation, John sees four angels "keeping a firm hold on the four winds of the earth, so that no wind would blow on the land or on the sea or on any tree" (Revelation 7:1), until God's servants are sealed. Both books picture winds as forces God keeps in check and releases for judgment (compare Jeremiah 49:36).

p: In the Bible too the east wind brings drought, scorching and locusts.
b: In the land of Israel the east wind blows off the desert, hot and dry. It scorches grain in Pharaoh's dream (Genesis 41:6), dries up springs (Hosea 13:15), withers vines (Ezekiel 17:10) and carries the locusts into Egypt (Exodus 10:13). Enoch's east wind brings "ruin, drought, heat and destruction."

p: Locust swarms ride the winds: Exodus and Joel knew it, and so does Enoch.
b: Desert locusts travel on the wind, sometimes hundreds of miles. An east wind brings them to Egypt and a west wind carries them away (Exodus 10:13–19). Joel describes a plague of them as an army (Joel 1–2). Enoch lists locusts among the gifts of several winds (76:9–11).

p: A north gate cannot lean south. The words may have been copied from 76:5 by mistake.
b: The seventh gate is the first of the north gates, on the east side, so "leans toward the south" makes no sense here. Both Dillmann's text and the EOTC print have it, so the Plain keeps it. Charles left it out. It may be a scribe's slip, copied from the description of the first east gate in 76:5.

p: The Astronomical Book is Enoch's teaching to his son, to be passed down the family line.
b: Enoch speaks here to his son Methuselah (Ge'ez Matusala), as again in 79:1 and 82:1. In Genesis, Methuselah is Enoch's son and Noah's grandfather (Genesis 5:21–29). The frame explains how the teaching could survive the flood: father to son, down to Noah. Jubilees says the same (Jubilees 7:38–39). Methuselah also appears in 1 Enoch's last chapters (see 106:4).

p: A wordplay that works in Hebrew and Aramaic, where qedem means both "east" and "before, first."
b: Ge'ez qädamawi, "first." The explanation only works in a Semitic original: Hebrew and Aramaic qedem means both "east" and "front, earlier time" (Genesis 2:8, "in the east"; Psalm 74:12, "from of old"). It is one sign that the Ge'ez goes back to a Hebrew or Aramaic book. "Quarter" in the Plain renders Ge'ez näfas, "wind," which here means a direction of the world.

a: the Most High will come down there
p: Behind the Ge'ez may lie a pun: Hebrew darom, "south," sounds like dar rom, "the High One dwells."
b: The Ge'ez says the Most High "will come down" in the south. Milik (1976) read the broken Aramaic of this verse (in his edition, 4Q209 fragment 23, with 4Q210) as saying that the south is called darom because the Great One "dwells" (dar) there; see the variant here. That is known here only from Milik's report and those who follow him, not checked against the edition. The explanation of darom as dar rom, "the High One dwells," is an older Hebrew wordplay. The Bible also has God come from the south, from Teman and Sinai (Deuteronomy 33:2; Habakkuk 3:3), and 1 Enoch puts God's throne mountain in the south (see 25:3).
orig: ልዑል ህየ ይወርድ (ləʿul həyä yəwärd), "the Most High there will descend"

p: Ge'ez nətug, "diminished," names the west as the place where all lights go down.
b: Nətug means "diminished, waning." Hebrew names the west ma'arav, from a verb for the sun going in or setting. In both, the west is where light ends each day.

p: Enoch places the garden of righteousness in the far north. Genesis puts Eden in the east.
b: Enoch visits "the garden of righteousness" in 32:3, and the Parables place the righteous and the chosen there (see 60:8; 61:12; 70:3). Genesis puts the garden "in Eden, toward the east" (Genesis 2:8). Here it is in the north, beside the dark seas, a hidden place at the edge of the world. In Hebrew and Aramaic, "north" (tsafon) sounds like "hidden" (tsafun).

p: Enoch saw seven great mountains on his earlier journeys too.
b: The Book of the Watchers also describes seven mountains (see 18:6–8; 24:2). Here frost comes from them, as in Job, where cold comes on the winds and ice appears when God breathes (Job 37:9–10). The mountains also seem to mark the turning of the seasons.

t: The Great Sea and the Erythraean Sea
p: The Great Sea is the Mediterranean. The Erythraean Sea is the Red Sea and the waters beyond it.
b: "The Great Sea" is the Bible's name for the Mediterranean (Numbers 34:6; Joshua 1:4). The "Erythraean Sea" (77:6–7) is the Greek name for the Red Sea, the Persian Gulf and the Indian Ocean together. The seven great rivers are not named; scholars have guessed at the Nile, Tigris, Euphrates and others. The map is the world as people in the Near East knew it after Alexander.

a: some say they empty into the desert
p: The writer reports another opinion, like a careful geographer.
b: The Ge'ez wäybelu, "and they say," marks a second view about where the rivers end. A writer who reports other opinions is not inventing freely but passing on geography he has learned. Some rivers of Arabia and Iran do run out into the desert instead of a sea. A tiny Greek papyrus scrap from Egypt (P.Oxy. 2069) was identified by Milik (1971) as containing a few words of 77:7–78:1 and 78:8. The scraps are very small, and some scholars, such as Knibb, doubt this identification more than Milik's identification of other scraps as 85:10–86:2 and 87:1–3.

p: The names look like Hebrew words for the sun, worn down in copying.
b: Charles suggested that Oryares comes from Hebrew 'or cheres, "light of the sun" (cheres is a poetic word for the sun, Job 9:7), and that Tomas may come from chammah, "the hot one," another word for the sun (Isaiah 30:26). These are guesses. The names were carried from Hebrew or Aramaic into Greek and then Ge'ez, and they wore down on the way.

p: The four names may reflect Hebrew words for the moon: yareach, levanah, keseh.
b: Charles guessed that Erae comes from Hebrew yareach, "moon," Ebla from levanah, "the white one" (Isaiah 24:23), and Benase from ben keseh, "son of the full moon" (keseh is the full moon of Psalm 81:3). Asonya is unexplained. The two names of the sun and four of the moon may stand for its phases or seasons, but the text does not say.

p: Here the moon has fifteen parts, not fourteen. The Ge'ez says "three fifths," or "three fives."
b: Chapter 73 counts the moon in fourteenths; here it seems to be counted in fifteenths. The Ge'ez has śälästu təḫməstä, which looks like "three fifths" but is best taken as "three fives," fifteen. The waning list in 78:8 starts at fourteen and ends with the fifteenth day. Babylonian tables of the moon's visibility (in the omen series Enuma Anu Enlil, Tablet 14) also count in fifteenths, which may be where this scheme came from (Drawnel; Ben-Dov).

a: on the first day it goes down to fourteen parts
p: A day-by-day table, like the ones Babylonian scribes kept.
b: The verse counts down day by day, from full moon to dark moon, one part a day. It is a lesson in counting, not a poem, and it reads like the tables of Babylonian scribes. The Aramaic copies at Qumran had long tables of this kind (see the note on 73:1).

a: twenty-nine days each, and at times twenty-eight
p: The real moon month is 29½ days, so moon calendars alternate months of 29 and 30.
b: From one new moon to the next is about 29½ days. A moon calendar therefore alternates months of 30 and 29 days, as 78:15–16 says: six of each make 354 days. A month of 28 days does not fit the real moon; it may be a slip, or a way of counting only the nights the moon is seen.

p: The Ge'ez calls the new moon śärq, "rising." In the Bible new moons were holy days.
b: Śärq means "rising": the day the light "rises" on the moon. In Israel the new moon was a holy day with its own offerings (Numbers 28:11–15), a day off from trade (Amos 8:5), a day to visit the prophet (2 Kings 4:23). Isaiah says all people will worship "from new moon to new moon" (Isaiah 66:23), and Paul mentions new moons among the holy days (Colossians 2:16).
r: Numbers 28:11–15; 1 Samuel 20:5; 2 Kings 4:23; Amos 8:5; Isaiah 66:23; Colossians 2:16

a: It becomes full exactly on the day
p: In a moon calendar, Passover and Booths fall at the full moon. In the 364-day year they need not.
b: The full moon rises at sunset opposite the sun, just as the verse says. In the Torah's calendar the two great feasts begin on the 15th of a month (Leviticus 23:6; Leviticus 23:34), which in a moon calendar is the full moon. In the 364-day calendar the 15th is a fixed day of the week, not tied to the moon. The rabbis' calendar kept the moon; Jubilees and the Qumran texts kept the sun's 364 days.

p: 177 days is three months of 30 and three of 29: half of a 354-day moon year.
b: 3 × 30 + 3 × 29 = 177, half of the 354-day moon year. Half of the 364-day year is 182 days, so in each half year the moon falls 5 days behind, as 79:5 says. 79:4 counts the same 177 days as "twenty-five weeks and two days."

p: The words are obscure. They may describe a face seen in the moon, or the text may be damaged.
b: The Ge'ez says the moon at night looks "like a man" (bəʾsi) "for twenty, each" and by day "like the sky." No one has explained it with confidence. It may mean the face people see in the full moon, and the pale moon in the daytime sky; or the text may have been damaged in copying.

p: Ge'ez says "Sabbaths," meaning weeks, as the Bible sometimes does.
b: Sänbätat means "Sabbaths" and here means weeks. The Bible uses the word the same way: "seven complete Sabbaths" are seven weeks (Leviticus 23:15), and the Pharisee fasts "twice a Sabbath," twice a week (Luke 18:12). The week matters in this calendar because 364 days is exactly 52 of them (72:32).

a: In the days of the sinners the years will be shortened.
p: Chapters 80–81 change tone: from tables to warnings. Many scholars think they were added later.
b: Up to now the book has been calm and technical. Chapter 80 is poetry about sin and disorder, and chapter 81 about the heavenly tablets and Enoch's last year. No Aramaic fragment of chapters 80–81 has been identified, and many scholars think these chapters were added when the Astronomical Book was joined to the rest of 1 Enoch. Others think 80:2–8 belonged to the book from the start, as a warning to those who keep the wrong calendar. Ethiopian Orthodox readers take the chapters as one revelation.

p: Jesus speaks of days "cut short" in the last trouble; 4 Ezra of years that hurry.
b: In the Gospels, Jesus says that unless the Lord had cut short those days of distress, no one would survive (Mark 13:20; Matthew 24:22). 4 Ezra says the age is hurrying to its end (4 Ezra 4:26). In Enoch the shortening is a sign of a world falling out of order because of sin, not God's mercy. The cosmic signs that follow (80:4–7) are like those in Mark 13:24–25 and Joel 2:10.

a: The rain will be held back
p: In the Torah, rain held back is the punishment for turning to other gods.
b: Deuteronomy warns that if Israel serves other gods, the LORD will "shut up the sky" so there is no rain (Deuteronomy 11:16–17). Elijah's drought (1 Kings 17:1; James 5:17) and the two witnesses of Revelation (Revelation 11:6) follow the same pattern. Enoch links the drought to the same sin: treating the stars as gods (80:7).

a: drought will come at the edge of the great chariot in the west
p: The Ge'ez has "the sky" and "drought." Charles read "the sun" and "in the evening."
b: Dillmann's text says "the sky will be seen," and the word ʿabar most likely means "drought, barrenness" (Leslau). Charles read "the sun shall be seen" and "he shall journey in the evening," taking the verse to describe the sun out of place. The Plain follows the Ge'ez as it stands. Either way, the light shines "more brightly than the order of light allows": the sky has broken its law.

a: Many of the leaders of the stars will stray from the command
p: Stars that leave their path are punished in 1 Enoch. Jude calls false teachers "wandering stars."
b: In 1 Enoch stars are living servants who can disobey. Enoch earlier saw stars bound and punished for not rising at their time (see 18:13–16; 21:3–6), and in the Animal Apocalypse fallen stars stand for the Watchers (see 86:1–3). Jude, who quotes 1 Enoch, calls false teachers "wandering stars, for whom the gloom of darkness has been kept forever" (Jude 13), probably drawing on this picture.

t: Compared with the Bible: star worship
p: Here Enoch and the Bible fully agree: the stars are made things, and worshiping them is sin.
b: Deuteronomy warns Israel not to look at "the sun, the moon and the stars, the whole army of the sky," and "bow down to them and serve them" (Deuteronomy 4:19). Kings bowed to the army of the sky anyway (2 Kings 21:3), and Josiah removed their priests (2 Kings 23:5). Paul says people exchanged the Creator for created things (Romans 1:25). Here 1 Enoch agrees with the 66 books, and every church reads this warning the same way.
r: Deuteronomy 4:19; Deuteronomy 17:3; 2 Kings 21:3; 2 Kings 23:5; Jeremiah 8:2; Romans 1:25

a: the book of the heavenly tablets
p: Tablets in heaven on which all deeds, and all history, are already written.
b: Ge'ez ṣäfṣäfä sämay, "tablets of heaven." The same phrase returns in 93:2, 103:2 and 106:19. Jubilees often says that a law or an event is "written on the heavenly tablets" (Jubilees 3:10; Jubilees 5:13; Jubilees 16:9). The Bible knows heavenly books: of names (Exodus 32:32), of days not yet lived (Psalm 139:16), of deeds opened at the judgment (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12), and "the book of truth" (Daniel 10:21).
orig: መጽሐፈ ዘጸፍጸፈ ሰማይ (mäṣḥäfä zäṣäfṣäfä sämay), "the book of the tablets of heaven"
r: Exodus 32:32; Psalm 139:16; Daniel 7:10; Daniel 10:21; Revelation 20:12; Jubilees 5:13; 93:2; 103:2; 106:19

a: all the deeds of human beings
t: Compared with the Bible: history written in advance
p: The Bible has books of deeds opened at the judgment. Enoch reads all of history before it happens.
b: Daniel and Revelation see books opened at the judgment (Daniel 7:10; Revelation 20:12), and a psalm says all one's days were written in God's book before one of them came (Psalm 139:16). Enoch goes further: he reads the deeds of every human being to the last generation. Many readers hear in this a strong idea of fate. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers read it as God's foreknowledge, which the Bible also affirms (Isaiah 46:10); other readers see it as going beyond what the 66 books say.

p: Psalm 24's title for God, and close to Paul's "King of the ages."
b: "Who is he, this King of glory? The LORD of Armies" (Psalm 24:10). Paul blesses "the King of the ages" (1 Timothy 1:17). Enoch's praise answers what he has just read: the God who made the sky's order also keeps the record of every life.

p: Enoch has just read all human sin, and he praises God for being patient.
b: Having read every deed of humankind, Enoch thanks God not for justice but for patience (təʾgəśt). The Bible praises the God who is "slow to anger" (Exodus 34:6), whose patience is meant to lead to repentance (Romans 2:4), and who waits, "not wanting anyone to perish" (2 Peter 3:9).

p: The Ge'ez can mean Enoch blessed God for humans' sake, or blessed humans themselves.
b: The Ge'ez baräku dibä is literally "I blessed upon" the children of the world. Charles understood it as "blessed Him because of the children of men." It can also mean that Enoch, like a priest, spoke a blessing over humankind. The Plain keeps the second, more literal sense.

a: Blessed is the man who dies righteous and good
t: A blessing on the righteous dead
p: Like Psalm 1 and Revelation 14:13, this blesses those who die faithful.
b: The saying is built like Psalm 1:1. Balaam wishes, "May I die the way the upright die" (Numbers 23:10). Revelation hears a voice from heaven say, "Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord from now on" (Revelation 14:13). In Enoch the righteous person's blessing is that the heavenly books hold nothing against him.

a: no flesh is righteous before the Lord
t: Compared with the Bible: no one is righteous
p: This matches Psalm 143:2, which Paul quotes: no living person is righteous before God.
b: "No one alive is righteous before you," prays the psalmist (Psalm 143:2), and Paul builds on that verse: by works of the law "no flesh" will be made righteous (Romans 3:20; Galatians 2:16). Job and Ecclesiastes say the same (Job 4:17; Ecclesiastes 7:20). So this agrees with the 66 books. Enoch's reason is that God is their Creator: the creature cannot stand as righteous before the one who made him. It sits beside 81:4, which blesses the righteous: Enoch, like the Bible, holds both.

a: In the second year they will take you away from among them
p: Genesis says only "God took him." Here Enoch gets one more year to teach his family.
b: Genesis says, "Enoch walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24); Hebrews says he was taken so he would not see death (Hebrews 11:5). 1 Enoch fills the gap: one last year at home to write and teach. Other parts tell of his final taking (see 70:1–4; 87:3). Jubilees also has Enoch taken to Eden to write (Jubilees 4:23).

a: they will be gathered in because of the deeds of the wicked
p: Isaiah says the righteous are taken away from evil. Wisdom of Solomon says it of Enoch.
b: "The righteous person perishes, and no one takes it to heart... the righteous is taken away from evil" (Isaiah 57:1). The Wisdom of Solomon speaks of one who pleased God and "was taken up," snatched away "so that evil would not change his mind" (Wisdom of Solomon 4:10–11), words most readers apply to Enoch. Here the righteous die because of others' sins, and "gathered in" (yətgabbəʾu) is the word for being gathered to one's people at death.

p: Ge'ez ʿalämat means both "worlds" and "ages."
b: ʾƎgziʾa ʿalämat is "Lord of the worlds" or "Lord of the ages": the word, like Hebrew ʿolam, covers both space and time. The Plain uses "ages," as in Paul's "King of the ages" (1 Timothy 1:17).

a: keep the books your father wrote with his own hand
p: The book explains its own survival: Enoch wrote, Methuselah kept, and the family handed it on.
b: Enoch gives his written books to Methuselah to hand on "to the generations of the world." Jubilees tells the same chain: Enoch taught Methuselah, Methuselah taught Lamech, and Lamech taught Noah (Jubilees 7:38–39), and Noah's books passed to Shem (Jubilees 10:14). Ethiopian Orthodox tradition accepts that Enoch's writings were preserved this way. Most historians read the chain as the book's way of explaining how a writing of the 200s BC could claim to come from before the flood.

a: this wisdom that is beyond their thoughts
p: God's thoughts are higher than ours (Isaiah 55:8–9); Paul speaks of a hidden wisdom (1 Corinthians 2:7).
b: For Enoch, knowing the true order of the sky is wisdom (ṭəbäb), a gift from God that human minds could not reach alone. Isaiah says God's thoughts are higher than ours (Isaiah 55:8–9). Paul speaks of God's wisdom, hidden and now revealed (1 Corinthians 2:7–10). In Enoch the revealed wisdom includes the calendar.

a: It will taste better to those who eat it than fine food
p: God's word is sweeter than honey in the Psalms; Ezekiel and John eat a scroll.
b: The psalms call God's rulings sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:10; Psalm 119:103). Ezekiel eats a scroll that tastes sweet as honey (Ezekiel 3:3), and so does John (Revelation 10:9–10). Enoch uses the same picture for his books: wisdom to be eaten, and the reader who has it "will not sleep."

a: do not sin as the sinners do in counting all their days
t: Compared with the Bible: is the calendar a matter of sin?
p: For Enoch a wrong calendar is sin. Paul tells Christians not to judge each other over days.
b: Here righteousness includes counting the year right. Jubilees agrees (Jubilees 6:32–38). The Torah does command that feasts be kept at their "appointed times" (Leviticus 23:4), but it never sets the calendar's rules. Paul writes, "Do not let anyone judge you about food and drink or about a feast day, a new moon or Sabbaths" (Colossians 2:16; compare Romans 14:5–6). So Enoch goes beyond the 66 books here, and many Christian readers think it conflicts with Paul. The Ethiopian Orthodox Church keeps its own fixed calendar of feasts and fasts, and its teachers read these verses as a call to keep God's order faithfully, not as a rule for the 364-day year.

p: Ge'ez näfḥä dibeyä, "he breathed upon me." The text does not say what the breath gave.
b: Uriel "breathed upon" Enoch (näfḥä dibeyä). The verse does not explain the act. Readers compare other breathings: God breathes life into the first human (Genesis 2:7), and Jesus breathes on his disciples as he gives the Spirit (John 20:22). Some see here a claim that Enoch's knowledge came by angelic gift, not study, as 82:7 as a whole implies.
orig: ነፍሐ ዲቤየ (näfḥä dibeyä), "he breathed upon me"

t: The feasts on the right days
p: Enoch never names a feast, but the books that follow him fix every feast on a weekday.
b: The Astronomical Book mentions "feasts" (bäʿalat) but never names one. Jubilees and the Qumran scrolls put every feast on the 364-day year, starting the year on a Wednesday, the day the lights were made (Genesis 1:14–19). Passover (the 14th of month 1) then always falls on a Tuesday, the Feast of Weeks (the 15th of month 3) on a Sunday, and the Day of Atonement (the 10th of month 7) on a Friday. A list in the Qumran scroll 4Q394 begins with the same 364-day year.

p: The Ge'ez says 364 here, but the officers seem to cover only 360 days. Charles wrote 360.
b: The heads of thousands divide the ordinary days, and the season leaders rule the four added days. So the officers' share should be 360 days, and Charles printed "three hundred and sixty." Dillmann's text and the EOTC print both say 364. The Plain keeps the Ge'ez; the number may count the whole year, with the four added days explained in the next clause.

p: Angel names built like Hebrew names, most ending in -el, "God."
b: These four rule the four seasons. Most of the names end in -el, "God," like Michael and Gabriel. Milkiel probably means "my king is God"; Narel may come from Hebrew ner, "lamp." The spellings differ between manuscripts (see the variant here), and their meanings are guesses. Only the first two seasons are described before the text breaks off (82:15–20).

a: At the beginning of the year
p: The year begins in spring, with 91 days: three months and an added day.
b: Each season lasts 91 days: three months of 30 days and one added day (72:13), so 4 × 91 = 364. Milkiel rules the first, from the spring equinox. He is also called Tamaini, a name no one has explained, and "Sun."

p: The Ge'ez word usually means "grief." Charles took it as "calm."
b: The Ge'ez lists ḥäf, "sweat," moq, "heat," and ḥazan, which normally means "grief, sorrow." Charles rendered "calms," thinking of still, heavy days. The Plain's "heaviness" tries to keep both the feeling and the weather.

p: Wheat harvest in spring, grapes and lambs in summer: the seasons fit Judea, not Ethiopia.
b: In the land of Israel wheat is cut in late spring, around the Feast of Weeks (Exodus 34:22), and grapes are trodden in late summer (Judges 9:27; 82:19). Flocks are bred in summer. These signs fit the farming year of Judea and are one more clue to where the book was written.

a: the trees of the rainy season
p: Kərämt is the Ethiopian rainy season: the translator's own word for winter.
b: Ge'ez kərämt names the great rainy season of the Ethiopian highlands. The translator used it for the season that in Judea is winter, the time of rain. It is a small trace of the people who carried this book into Ge'ez.

a: the days of his rule are complete
p: The Ge'ez stops after two seasons. The rest is lost, though the Aramaic may have kept some of it.
b: Enoch has described spring and summer but not autumn and winter, and the Ethiopic stops here. Something has been lost. The Aramaic scroll 4Q211 contains parts of a description of the seasons and stars that does not appear in the Ethiopic, and Milik thought it came from the lost ending. Chapter 83 begins a new work, the Dream Visions.
